rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all eight compounds and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The intermediate temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.
Raise temperature while keeping the gradient unchanged to test selectivity of the only unresolved pair. This should also shorten retention, preserving the current zero time penalty.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. Keep temperature and solvent endpoints fixed to isolate the effect of slope on the limiting pair.

Slightly reduce the slope relative to injection 3 to recover resolution of the first pair while remaining faster than injection 2. The lower endpoint is still well above the observed last-peak elution composition.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to trim early low-strength time, while slightly flattening the gradient to protect the limiting pair. This tests whether the fully resolved separation can finish sooner than injection 4.

Use a slope just steeper than injection 4, targeting a slightly faster separation while retaining R ≥ 1.5 for the first pair. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition of about 0.57.

Test a slightly steeper slope near the first pair’s resolution threshold, with an earlier transition to the final hold. The last peak may elute briefly into the hold; compare its retention time with injection 6 while checking that full resolution is preserved.

Probe the low-temperature selectivity regime, where the critical early pair may separate in the opposite order. A steeper gradient offsets increased retention and tests an alternative route to a faster fully resolved method.

Shorten the low-temperature gradient to test whether the late three-peak cluster separates with a change in slope. The early pair has some resolution margin, and the shorter gradient should reduce the last retention time.

The late cluster barely responded to slope at 25 C, so raise temperature one step to change its selectivity. Returning to the 8-minute gradient gives the early pair more resolution margin while testing this intermediate-temperature compromise.

Return to the successful high-temperature regime and slightly flatten injection 5’s gradient to recover its marginal early-pair resolution. This tests whether the higher starting organic fraction can support another fully resolved, short method.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction improves early-pair selectivity in the intermediate-temperature regime. At 35 C, the late cluster should separate more than at 30 C, while the trimmed gradient window limits retention time.

Test the remaining grid point between injections 3 and 4 to pinpoint the steepest fully resolving gradient at 60 C. The first pair is expected to be near R = 1.5, with a last peak slightly earlier than injection 7 if resolution holds.

The fastest fully resolved method is close to the resolution threshold; test a shallower gradient for greater resolution margin while retaining the maximum CRF. Based on the observed retention trend, the last peak should still elute before 10 minutes.

Balance the opposing slope responses of the early pair and the third–fourth pair using a gradient between injections 2 and 14. This should preserve maximum CRF with stronger minimum-resolution margin than the fastest method and shorter retention than injection 14.

Trim the starting solvent window of injection 15 to shorten retention while using its resolution margin to protect the early pair. This tests a faster alternative with more separation margin than the near-threshold six-minute gradient.

Shorten injection 16 by one gradient-time step to approach the resolution boundary at this starting composition. Injection 11 suggests the resulting slope should leave the early pair close to R = 1.5 while reducing the last retention time.

Flatten injection 12’s gradient to improve its sole unresolved pair while retaining the higher starting organic fraction. This tests whether the intermediate-temperature regime can also achieve full resolution before the 10-minute time penalty begins.

Lower the starting organic fraction and slightly flatten the slope relative to injection 18 to recover early-pair resolution. This targets a fully resolved, lower-temperature alternative with the last peak still expected before 10 minutes.

Trim the unused high-organic portion of injection 11 while keeping a slightly shallower slope to protect the limiting pair. This should preserve maximum CRF with an eight-minute programmed gradient and all peaks eluting before the final hold.

Test a compromise between injection 7’s speed and injection 15’s resolution margin using a narrower solvent window. The shallower slope should strengthen the limiting early pair while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes and near the end of the programmed gradient.

Increase the endpoint one step from injection 21 to shorten retention while retaining early-pair resolution margin. This slope matches the successful injection 2 but removes unused high-organic gradient time.

Test a shallower, trimmed gradient near the balance point between the two slope-sensitive early pairs. This should retain maximum CRF with roughly R = 2 minimum resolution and the last peak before 10 minutes.

Steepen injection 23’s gradient to shorten retention while preserving a useful resolution margin for both early critical pairs. The observed slope response predicts full resolution and a last peak around 7.9 minutes, retaining maximum CRF.

Shorten retention relative to injection 24 with one endpoint step while preserving the demonstrated resolving slope of injection 2. This final method is expected to retain the maximum CRF, with minimum resolution about 1.67 and the last peak near 7.49 minutes.
